title: Panthers Live Press Conference
text: Heat. Heat. Heat. Heat. N. Hey, hey, hey. Hey. [music] Hey. Hey. >> [music] >> Oh, Oh. Oh, heat. >> Ei. Down here. >> Heat. Heat. Hallelujah. Hey, heat. Hey, heat. >> Heat. Heat. Another great day on the grass. Um just really excited for this weekend. Excited to be back in Bank of America Stadium in front of our fan base. Uh the energy, all the things that come with it and um just taking the next step as a team, a championship. Truly a championship opportunity with the division opponent. We're so excited about it and uh can't wait for it. >> How did Monroe kind of progress this week? >> He looked great. Uh he did an excellent job. um you know working in there, working back um after the knee and um you know he was had a lot of energy today and was excited to be out there and and uh you know get involved in some different ways. So um excited about Monroe. >> You had said there were some different scenarios to work through with him. >> Yeah. >> Will you continue to roll with Rasheed and Teemo for the time being? >> Well, I don't want to comment on that right now just because we have possibilities. So, um, but you know, just for for all intents purposes, he he looked great this week, you know, so he'll he'll uh have a chance to really help us. Dave, you guys are last in the league in first half rushing, but second best in second half rushing. You're going up against um the number two run defense like how do you guys find momentum early when you want to stay balanced? >> Yeah. Um that's been the that's been the uh the the real challenge for the group to figure out, you know, how do we get that part rolling? Um, and again, you look back at last weekend, we rip off an 11-yd run on the first play and um, you know, I was pretty excited to see where that was going to trend. And then also, you got to give your opponents some due. Um, the Eagles, that's a really good defense and, uh, really stout front. Coach Bowls, that group, they really know how to play the run and, uh, it's a big emphasis for them. The physicality of the way they play it and, um, attacking their gaps and different things, they'll create some challenges, you know, and I I believe it's just about consistency. Um, our guys find a way to settle in. It's part of our nature. We just keep playing, keep figuring out the information, finding ways to run the ball with efficiency, you know, which continued to improve in the second half. But how can we get that going all the way throughout to create that balance? That is the the focus. >> Dave, as you predicted, Todd just said, Baker's going to start is going to wear custom glove. just your thoughts on playing him and uh I don't know whether he's going to be compromised or not but going to be wearing a glove. >> You know, I kind of figured that would be the case. Um just knowing Baker and uh the toughness that he showed in the time that I spent with him uh being able to play through things, wanting to be out there with his teammates. So, I don't expect I didn't expect anything less. Um and again with the glove, I'm not really sure. We did have a similar situation in Seattle. Um I don't know if you guys remember Russell hurt his middle finger. um missed a couple of games, came back at Green Bay and really wanted to be out there with his teammates and in the meantime, you know, Gina was out there and playing well too um in hisstead. So, uh the guys have motivation really. They want to win and and they certainly want to be the guy out there and and so I'm I'm counting on that approach from Baker. >> Tampa's had three offensive coordinators in three years. Um game planning this week, was it easier uh than like previous years because Zack was already an offensive coordinator in the division. You guys have an idea of the kind of stuff that he wants to do. >> Yeah, there's uh there's some similarities with what he was doing in Atlanta to what he's doing now. There's still a lot of the uh concepts that really me, Goodie, Baker, Brad. Um and then of course what Liam brought to Tampa, there's still a lot of that um in the core of what they're doing. Um, and that's smart to do. When you have a quarterback who's functioning at a high level, playing really quality football, you want to keep him there. But at the same time, Zach's got a lot to bring and he did some amazing things, you know, with uh Bjang and in different ways, making him come alive. And then, of course, you now you got Bucky. So, you have another player to kind of fit into that mold and the way they try to get him the ball. Um, there are some similarities. So, we kind of take all that into consideration and and really kind of look at what they've done in in the last couple of weeks, too. >> Go ahead. You talked about wanting [clears throat] the running game to start fast in the first half as well, but what's the balance and and wanting it to start fast and being patient and understanding like you can wear down a defense so like you don't want to get away from it either. >> Yeah, that's the philosophy. Um and that's something that I was handed down from, you know, from Pete, from Coach Carol and it was this belief that he never was saying, "Hey, we got to establish the run, but the runs should be more efficient than they've been." And that's really what I'm looking for. Um, would I love explosive runs? Absolutely those happen, but you really want that efficient run. So, you're in second and normal and you got your whole call sheet. As a play caller, just for everybody, just, you know, when you're in that second and six or less, you can pretty much call anything that creates indecision on the defense. It creates uh an attacking mindset. When you start to get into the second and longers, yes, you should run it some, but the best way to get half back is to be able to pass the ball and do other things as well. So, um, that's kind of leaguewide. Um, so that's really what we're looking for. Looking for that efficiency to happen, you know, where you're getting those threes and fours early on because everything's blocked, right? Versus, you know, somebody slips off of a combo or maybe the back misses the the hole or the cut. A lot of different things um happen that way. And it's [snorts] kind of like this settling in where how is this defensive front trying to play us today? Are they are they stunting a lot? Are they blitzing with the interior linebackers? Are they using edge pressure to attack you in the run game? And once you kind of figure those things out, you come to the sideline, you troubleshoot, you continue to get better and better. And my my note to Brad is by the end of this game, let's make sure we've run it well. And that's what's been happening. You know, it's um it's this kind of gradually getting stronger, then all of a sudden you end up with 120, 150 yards by the end of it. That's great. You know, when you have the balance early on, then you become more dangerous, more explosive because you can throw play actions and things like that. When you guys brought up Trey this week, um AJ doesn't have a status. He hasn't really played on special teams much since the season started, but played well during the preseason. >> Are you going to run with four running backs active from now on? Is that kind of the way you see it going? You know, bringing up Trey when he had practice squad elevations. >> It's a possibility. Um but Trey's done a great job on special teams. So, um, and in fact, you know, AJ had a punt cover tackle, you know, a couple games ago when he was out there. So, um, he's done a good job. He's willing to and he wants to continue to do that. Trey's made an impact. He returns, he blocked the punt, he covers well. Um, he's really emerging as like guys that we've had in the past, DJ Dallas, Travis Homer. These are guys that like you trust them when they're in there for the protection and run the ball if you need them to, but in the meantime, they're returning, they're covering, they're rushing, they're blocking, they're doing all the different things that a third running back can, as we all know, it's hard to give three people the ball. One person, the second guy comes in and gets his touches as well. Um, but when you have that to consider, and all the other positions that have needs, that's when you got to say, okay, if somebody's going to be up on game day, can we use them and how can we use them? Do you know whether you're going to activate BAM? >> Uh it's a possibility. Yeah. You know, um really what the opportunity that opens itself up for BAM is, you know, is uh Thomas Inkum being out right now. And so, you know, there's a couple of guys that can kind of fill those roles. It's Nick Hampton, it's it's Bam, Martin Scott, you know, um nobody, you know, certainly the the leadership, the energy, and all those things that TI brings, that's hard to replace. We're looking for guys that can come in and fill those roles um and that void that he leaves. >> Dave, since you've been with [clears throat] the Panthers, uh you've played the Bucks four times. Three of those four have been one-score games. >> What do you think, why do you think these games come down to the wire so much uh between these two particular teams? >> It's a division opponent first and foremost. So, um you know, we love those division games. Um they're very physical. that usually battling who's get who has the ball last, you know, and you're fighting and scratching. Um, being able to spend time with coach BS um, you know, being able to go against his defense, coach knowing what we're doing in different ways, trying to offset those things and use the information that we we both might have. They know that we know that they know that we know that they know and you kind of go back and forth, you know, in different situations that way. But, um, you know, a a coach, an organization, you know, Jason Light, the whole thing, the players, um, the guys that I was able to spend time with, there's a lot of lot lot of respect. Um, and it also just kind of heightens the competition of the moments because of that. So, um, I think that probably plays into it some. >> Saw JC out there today. How's how's he doing, would you say? >> JC is doing great. Um, the reports I get are that he's trending in the right direction. um you know, ahead of whatever you know, general deadlines, he's he's crushing his rehab right now. He's he's itching to just keep taking the next step. Mike Jack, same thing. Um you know, he's he's moving around. They're starting to pick up their their speeds, the change of direction stuff. Those are all the things, you know, with the nature of the injuries that have to feel really good um before you're able to open up. Obviously, you got to go through the four games. Um and then after that you you start thinking about opening up windows when they can function and do their job, you know. And the last part of it is really that violent change of direction. Those things um really are the limiting factors with a core muscle injury, with a quad injury, those types of um those types of injuries, you know, it's like you can start building strength, you can start building linear speed, but you got to be able to move in this game. So, um that'll be the next stride for those guys. And uh Brooks as well. Is Cam Jackson the only guy that's been injured in season that you guys view as a season ending injury on IR at this point? >> I believe so. Um, yeah. And that's just, you know, the nature of the surgery, the time it takes to rehab and all that. >> Everybody good? >> All right. Thank you. >> Thanks, D.

title: Sam LaPorta meets with the media | October 23, 2026
text: What is your reaction to how your comments on "Pardon My Take" were perceived, both by the fans and others? Yes, I feel bad if there was any kind of distraction for the team, my teammates, or the coaches, but I think maybe there was a bit of a misunderstanding with, um, I guess my intentions are that I want to play for this team.  I give everything I have .  My colleagues too.  Everyone loves me, respects me, and supports me, and I suppose they want to see me happy and well paid. So, can you explain, you know, your frustration?  Obviously, there is some frustration.  I think you already hinted at that a couple of weeks ago with us too.  Where does that come from, you know, with the negotiations? I guess I wouldn't expect anyone else to really care, but emotionally, for me and my family, it's a big deal.  Um, we want to have stability.  We are excited for the next few months, as my wife and I are expecting our first child .  We're going to welcome our baby into the world here in the Detroit metropolitan area.  You know, we want to be here with the Lions.  And I guess I'm getting carried away about it , but in the bigger picture, it's a business and you have to respect what management does because they're the ones who make the decisions.  They were the ones who brought me here.  It's my first team.  Um, they have always been very supportive of me and my career. Have you been able to separate the football aspect, you know, from the business side? Like the fact that you can continue playing and performing at the level you have been doing with all of this happening.  How have you managed to separate both aspects? Um, I guess you learn early in your career that you're employed and paid to do a good job for this team, and if you don't do a good job, you're not going to be here. Sam, if you understand the business side, as you said, do you feel bad that it became public? Do you regret that it came to light because you mixed the business side with the emotional one? Clear.  I don't know if I regret it.  Um, I just don't expect others to understand, and we're very lucky.  It's like I'm getting paid millions of dollars this year.  So we have to take it with caution.  Well, it's partly from a position where I'm looking for security for myself and my family, but also, when I reflect on others in the league, I feel like I do a job just as good, if not better, and I want to be paid the same as them. Since we last spoke, have there been any updates or have the talks resumed? Um, no, I don't think so. Hey Sam, you had your best game against Arizona and that was after the talks were cut off.  And are you finding ways to channel your frustration to bring even more intensity to the field in some way ?    I do n't believe it.  I haven't really changed the way I prepare.  Um, yes.  You know, I'm going to give it my all every week.  And you know, starting this weekend, there's a big game, trying to take the lead in the division, get 1-0 up and see what we can do from there. Did you expect this to blow up like it did? Um, I think the media always takes small stories and blows them out of proportion, and when they put comments together, everything can seem harsher or bigger than it actually is.  I am a piece in a gigantic machine, a huge cog in this building, and I want to continue doing my part; I hope something happens soon. Sam, can you explain where things stand with that?  I mean, where's your frustration? Is it because you do n't have an offer, the money, the guaranteed money? What exactly is going on with Um? I don't know if I should go into that because we'd be here all day, but you should ask my agent about that.

title: David Corrao meets with the media | October 23, 2026
text: Hey, let's start with Jimmy.  He had a small opportunity a couple of weeks ago, but we took it away from him a bit when other players recovered.    You know, maybe it didn't work out the way you wanted.  Development is not linear.  I think we all understand that. So, where do they see the value in that small opportunity they had, and how are they growing from it? Well, I mean, it's going to get better with more experience each week.  In other words, that's the natural progression, especially for a novice player. The things I've noticed, when I see him on special teams, are that he has an athleticism and physicality that will serve him well as a linebacker as well. And I think it's simply the process of gaining trust, of getting to know their work. We are still trying to define specific roles for this player. But I think Jimmy is showing that he can have a role for us in the game and contribute to a good result.  Do you think those special teams repetitions build confidence in young players simply by participating in NFL games and having to complete specific assignments? Does that translate to the offense or defense? I think the simple fact of being in the game, right?  That's the adjustment. You take these players from college to the NFL.  The speed of the game is different.  The style of play is different.  And for young players coming into the league, if they aren't undisputed starters from the beginning, special teams are a great way for them to avoid that look of awe of "oh my god, this is huge".  Jimmy has played high-level college football .  So that transition to special teams will really help him.  And I think he's done well with that. How important is Derek to the overall plan of what you want to do defensively?  Just look at his production: 27 tackles, four tackles for loss, two sacks, interceptions, one pass defended.  He does a little bit of everything for you. How important is that role, that position, and their versatility in what they do? Well, it's obvious that Derek is a very important player for us.  And that evolves over time, right? Every game is different, every match is different, and the things we have to ask him to do within our defensive scheme will change every week, you know, depending on who we're playing against and what they do.  Um, obviously, Derek is one of our most explosive and aggressive players, and we need to make sure that the list of tasks we ask him to do is what he does best ;  And every week we try to figure that out, um, and put him in that position so he can just play, because, I mean, you guys see it.  When that player is loose and decisive, and knows where to go and what to do, he makes many plays in our defense, and it's up to us to put him in that place where he can help us.    We 've heard a lot about confidence and doing your job as one of the main keys to correcting some of the initial mistakes.  What does Brian Branch do for linebackers, in terms of a holistic view of defense, when you have a player like that who you feel will fulfill his assignment play after play? Yes, I mean, you bring back a player of Brian Branch's caliber and that changes the whole unit.  I mean, this guy, again, makes game- changing plays.  I think it inspires confidence in everyone else out there with him.  Okay, BB is out there with us.  He 's doing his job, I have to do mine because when the play comes to him, he makes great plays that change the game.  So, that puts me in a position where I'm responsible to him, as well as the rest of the guys on the field, to do my job and make the plays that come my way. Looking at that performance in Arizona, when you observed and studied it, what do you think you did better overall as a unit compared to what you did perhaps in the first four games of the season, and how do you continue to do that going forward? Well, I think the execution was the most important thing, and the plan was the plan, you know, we came up with our plan .  I think the guys really believed in what we were doing.    We went out and executed it.  We said we have to do certain things on defense to eliminate what you do on defense, right?  The most important thing you have to do on defense is prevent the offense from doing what it does best, and who are its best players?  And I think our boys really understood what we were trying to do. And that's something we need to build on.  We need to build on this because what we did against Arizona isn't necessarily what we'll have to do against Green Bay.  I mean, we're talking about two totally different teams, two totally different quarterbacks, different receivers, different approaches to the game , different staff groups, and it's up to us.  That is the process for the defense.  We need to create a plan designed to give us the best chance of stopping what Green Bay does best. David, Jack Campbell has been quite critical of himself during the first three or four games.  He looked more like himself against the Cardinals and maybe he was just compensating for the players around him.  But how did you see their approach to the game, their execution in the game change for the better against Arizona? Well, I think he came back to playing football as he just came back to, instead of trying to be the guy who runs the show and tells everyone what to do, he runs our operation.  So, the responsibility falls on the other players to see that when he makes adjustments, when he makes decisions on the field, you as another player have to see it.  It's not up to him to tell you , it's up to you to understand it, and I think what made things easier for him was that our guys were much more focused on doing it that way.  And now that takes the pressure off. He does what he's supposed to do and now Jack is back to being Jack, playing football the way he knows how. With Campbell's performance, he did a lot of man-to-man coverage on Trey McBride.  It's not that we've never seen Jack go man-to- man, but I don't know if at that level against that caliber of opponent.  I know Dan said he wanted someone to walk into the locker room and demand that confrontation.  I don't know if Jack did anything as bold as that, but seeing the way he stepped up in something we might not know about him or his abilities, what can you build on that with him? Well, I mean, and we've talked about this in the past, you know, Jack is an American football player.  In other words, it's a legitimate type of football.  You give him time, you give him repetitions, you give him training.  I don't think there's anything that player can't do on the football field.  He's made to be a center back.  That is the prototype of a center back in modern football.  He can run, he can tackle, he can play in the zone, he has good instincts in the zone, and he can cover a big tight end.  I think what ultimately matters is, what is he getting repetitions on? What are we asking him to do?  And if he is clear and focused, that player will do what we ask of him and he will do it well . How have you seen Shep handle himself behind the scenes while navigating some of those early defensive difficulties ? You know, I think you know, he's the face of the defensive operation, right?    I mean , that's basically what it is.  But at the same time, he's not out there alone.  I think what I appreciate about him is how open he is with the other coaches on the staff. He knows he has Casey Rogers, perhaps the best defensive line coach, helping him with the front seven;  You know, you've got De'Shawn Towns and Jimmy O'Neal, the guys in the back.  I know Shep and I've worked with him, and I know, you know, I try to tell him what I think he needs to hear, not necessarily what he wants to hear, and I think that's what he's asking me for.  So what I've seen him do is navigate with the understanding that we have a process, right?  And the results are what we will be judged by, but the process has to be clean and efficient.  And I believe we have never deviated from our process. And I think that, as a second-year coordinator, has shown a level of ... I don't know if I want to call it experience, whatever you want to call it, where he doesn't... we're not making hasty decisions.  Like, "Oh, wow, this didn't work."  No, we have to continue with the process, continue training, continue working to find the things our boys do well and put them in that position. We talked so much about all the things BB does well, whether it's pressing, covering, dropping back, identifying and diagnosing, taking the ball away, all of that.  If you had to narrow it down to just one thing, what is the thing that makes you feel best? Well, I mean, I don't know.  I don't think it's like, "Oh, it's this particular thing."  I think that guy makes great plays.  I mean, he, he makes plays, whether it's defending against the run.  I mean, we can go over his career with, you know, great interceptions, hard hits, sacks, great tackles for loss, covering someone, you know.  I think it's simply a legitimate game creator.  Brian Branch makes plays.  That's what he does.

The marquee matchup, the game within the game, the chess match. It's the Texans all-pro corner Derek Stingley Jr. against fellow LSU football alum, New York Giants star wide receiver Malik Nabers. And this is a really interesting, intriguing matchup to me because of the elite athleticism, the shared alma mater, like storied college football program, the LSU Tigers, and the importance of the match up within this game. So, for the Texans whose defense has been obviously not up to the standard this season, and they're allowing a lot of yards, they're allowing a lot of passing touchdowns. They've been good against the run, but it's been the pass defense that's been suspect this year. So, that's why this match up is so central to this game because where is the Giants potential edge? It's throwing the football to Malik Nabers, and we'll get into the threat of tight end Isaiah Likely, but for the purpose of the beginning of this one, let's focus on Stingley versus Nabers. So, to me, this is it. And you see Derek Stingley Jr., his skills. We've been watching him for years. All Pro, the Texans 30-million-a-year man, 90-million overall, that big extension he signed a couple years ago. So, with Stingley, he's someone that obviously is capable of these big-time performances, shadowing wide receivers, but they don't do that that often. I still think they're going to match up quite a bit. And Malik Nabers, you see his explosion off the line of scrimmage, his size, the catch radius, the volume of catches, and how often he's targeted. So, we know right now the game plan. J.J. McCarthy, the New York Giants new quarterback, we'll get into some match up with him, the depth of him being inserted as the new starter after a good performance last week, replacing James Winston. So, you think about LSU, they call it DB University, but what about that lineage of LSU wide receivers? Guys like Justin Jefferson, and of course, Malik Nabers. So, this is not just your standard game day match up. This is a battle for supremacy, bragging rights, really a masterful situation in terms of elite athletic execution. So, breaking down the whole history, looking at everything that, you know, goes on when you're talking about the explosiveness of a Derek Stingley versus, you know, Malik Nabers. This is a tough one, but yeah, when Derek Stingley Jr., when he went to Baton Rouge, he was a true freshman and he dominated the SEC uh quarterbacks only allowed 41.1%of their passes targeting him, had six interceptions, 26 passes defended during that national championship run. An absolute prodigy. And then, Malik Nabers, they did not overlap as primary options at LSU. But, he left as LSU's all-time receiving yards leader, drafted sixth overall by the Giants 2024. And he really has built this reputation for an unteachable trait, sudden, violent ability to get open against any defensive back in single coverage. Well, that trait will be tested when Derek Stingley Jr. matches up with him, because Derek Stingley Jr. has a history, a track record of shutting down top wide receivers. So, technically, Derek Stingley Jr., looking at him, 6'1, 195, prototypical modern corner, really fluid hip transition, elite recovery speed, and he's widely considered one of the top man-to-man coverage corners in the entire NFL. When they let him, emphasis, when they let him lock into press man, he eliminates half the field. So, will they use that technique against Malik Nabers? Will they continue to play off? We're going to find out. And then, Malik Nabers, we see his footwork at the top of the routes, elite acceleration, and he's 6-foot, he's 200. A rare blend, twitchy route running, elite physical strength. A target monster, demands the football, chemistry with any quarterbacks turn the Giants offense to this It's a concentrated passing attack. You leave him alone on an island and his acceleration, his vertical burst, they can leave elite corners even gasping for air. So, thinking about his absolutely staggering workload over the last couple of weeks, in 3 weeks, six catches, 112 yards against Arizona. 11 catches on 20 targets, 121 yards against Washington Commanders. 12 catches for 15 uh sorry, for 165 yards on 15 targets against New Orleans Saints. 29 catches on 42 targets in the last 3 weeks, the Saints game being the last one. Definition of a high-volume alpha wide receiver. Hearing from the alpha, this guy's the alpha. He's the alpha receiver. And Derek Stingley Jr., he's now for corner. So, when guys like this match up, sometimes we want to shine a light on this and look at it. And from his side of the equation, you saw 15 passes defense last year, four interceptions. And now, they're playing more zone over 76%of the time, but they still clear out when Derek Stingley Jr.'s in that area. So, it's going to be interesting to see how they match this thing up strategically. So, in terms of the chess match, will DeMeco Ryans break the schematic tendencies? Will he let Derek Stingley Jr. travel in shadow coverage to follow Malik Nabers everywhere he goes? If Malik Nabers stays exclusively on the outside, Stingley is capable of taking away that deep boundary targets where Nabers has thrived. So, how will the Giants handle the intermediate stuff? He runs a heavy volume slants, intermediate crossers. They do that to maximize his yards after the catch. If Stingley's in zone, they'll have to pass Nabers off to the linebackers and safeties. So, the execution over the middle of the field will decide the game. If it's Caleb Bullock, yeah, you're in good hands. If it's linebackers, mm, maybe not. And if it's their are safety, MJ Stewart, starting with Reed Blankenship out with a concussion. It's a issue. Potentially. So, who wins the battle? So, this is what pro football's all about. Elite athletes from a big-time program in the Southeastern Conference, LSU playing at the peak of their powers. Technique for technique, speed for speed, will against will, skill against skill. So, does Stingley lock down the boundary, or does Malik Nabers, does he eat does he feast these high-volume targets and break loose? Is it going to be like that CeeDee Lamb game? What did the Texans learn from the 17-catch game-winning touchdown game from Mr. CeeDee Lamb from the Dallas Cowboys? You know, how do they learn from their mistakes?
